Objectives of the Financial System Report 
The Bank of Japan's Financial System Report has two main objectives. The first is to assess the 
stability of Japan's financial system. The second is to communicate with all related parties on the 
future tasks and challenges in order to ensure the system's stability. 
The Report assesses the vulnerabilities of the financial system from a macroprudential perspective. 
Within a macroprudential framework, institutional designs and policy measures are developed 
based on risk  assessments in the financial system  in order to ensure the stability of the overall 
financial system. In so doing, the interconnectedness of the real economy, financial markets, and 
financial institutions' behavior is taken into account. 
The Bank uses the results of the analysis set out in the Report in planning policies to ensure the 
stability of the financial system a nd for providing guidance and advice to financial institutions 
through on-site examinations and off-site monitoring. It makes use of the  results in international 
discussions on regulation, supervision, and vulnerability assessment. In relation to the conduct of 
monetary policy, the macro assessment of financial system stability is also regarded as important 
input for the Bank in assessing risks in economic and price developments from a medium- to long-
term perspective. 
Motivations behind the October 2026 issue 
In global and domestic financial markets, the expansion in global AI-related demand had the effect 
of improving market sentiment, although uncertainties remained high over the situation in the 
Middle East. Against this background, stock prices increased, and credit spreads on corporate 
bonds remained at low levels. However, uncertainties remain high over factors such as the future 
situation in the Middle East, the profitability and financing of AI -related investment, and 
developments in the foreign non-bank financial intermediary (NBFI) sector. This Report assesses 
the stability of the financial system under such an external environment. 
With regard to the foreign NBFI sector , private funds and other entities  have been playing an 
increasingly prominent role as providers of financing amid the substantial increase in global AI-
related investment. This Report examines these recent developments and, in its macro stress 
testing, refines the specification of the impact of a decline in expectations regarding the profitability 
of AI-related investment and assumes the situation where shocks are amplified mainly by portfolio 
adjustments in the foreign NBFI sector, thereby assessing the adequacy of banks' capital. 
While no major financial imbalances have been seen in the domestic financial cycle, developments 
in asset prices, such as real estate prices and stock prices, continue to warrant careful attention  
and close monitoring. Furthermore, the Report examines the effects of the rise in raw material and 
energy prices reflecting the situation in the Middle East  on small and medium -sized enterprises 
(SMEs), as well as the effects of interest rate increases on the corporate and household sectors . 
In addition, it assesses banks' profits and loss-absorbing capacity during the phase of policy rate 
hikes and examines issues surrounding loan and deposit management. 
Moreover, given that  advances in so -called "frontier AI" have further heightened cybersecurity 
threats, this Report reviews the efforts undertaken by financial institutions, financial authorities, and 
other relevant entities.

I. Executive summary: Stability assessment of Japan's financial system 
Japan's financial system has been maintaining stability on the whole. 
In the loan market, financial intermediation has continued to function smoothly as firms' demand 
for loans has continued to rise and banks' lending stance has remained active. Under these 
circumstances, no major financial imbalances have been seen in current financial activities. 
Japanese banks have sufficient capital bases and stable funding bases to withstand various stress 
situations, specifically including (1) stress equivalent to the global financial crisis that would cause 
major corrections  in financial markets and the real economy at home and abroad ; and (2) a 
compound stress of  the materialization of geopolitical risks such as  a rise in crude oil prices, 
together with a decline in expectations regarding AI, and a substantial rise in interest rates, all 
happening simultaneously. However, it is necessary to continue to carefully monitor the impact that 
factors such as the future situation in the Middle East, the profitability and financing of AI-related 
investment, and developments in the foreign non-bank financial intermediary (NBFI) sector have 
on the financial system through various channels . From a long -term perspective, if a structural 
decline in firms' loan demand, mainly reflecting the population decline, persists, banks' profitability 
and loss-absorbing capacity could decline, depending on the supply and demand balance in the 
loan market. This could lead to a contraction of financial intermediation activities or an overheating, 
such as an excessive search for yield. From the perspective of maintaining stability in Japan's 
financial system , close attention is warranted on future developments in the system, while 
examining both overheating and contraction risks (Chart I-1).

the heat map (Chart I-1). Nevertheless, in terms of stock valuations as of the end of September, 
price-earnings (P/E) ratios have remained broadly around their average levels since 2008, 
reflecting an increase in expected earnings per share (EPS), which is the denominator (left panel 
of Chart I -2). Risk premiums indicated by the equity yield spreads, i.e., the difference between 
expected equity yields and 10 -year Japanese government bond (JGB) yields, have declined 
somewhat amid rising interest rates, but have remained at relatively high levels from a somewhat 
longer-term perspective  (right panel of Chart I -2). Japanese stock prices have been rising, 
supported by expectations of profit improvements in sectors such as electric appliances, precision 
instruments, nonferrous metals, and machinery , which stand to benefit relatively more from  the 
ongoing global expansion in AI -related demand. Thus, Japanese stocks could face adjustment 
pressure if profits do not expand in line with large-scale AI-related investments by hyperscalers and

Foreign NBFI sector and AI-related investment → Chapters III, IV-A, V-B, and VI-B 
The presence of the foreign NBFI sector has expanded globally, raising concerns about risks such 
as the amplification of shocks in the event of stress. Although the share of financial assets held by 
the domestic NBFI sector in Japan is relatively low compared with other countries, there has been 
a steady increase in lending to and investment in the foreign NBFI sector by domestic banks, as 
well as in investments in Japanese stocks and bonds by the foreign NBFI sector, particularly those 
related to foreign funds (left panel of Chart I-4). Against this background, Japan's financial system 
may have become more susceptible to fluctuations in global financial markets and developments 
in foreign investment funds. 
Driven by strong expectations for growth in AI -related markets, hyperscalers , particularly in the 
United States , have significantly increased their business fixed investment recently. While 
hyperscalers have traditionally financed data center investment with their internal funds, they have 
recently increased external financing mainly through corporate bond issuance and have 
increasingly sought to secure rights to use third -party data centers via long -term lease 
commitments (middle and right panels of Chart I -4). Against this background, foreign NBFIs, 
including private funds, have been playing an increasingly prominent role as providers of financing 
for the part of such investment that hyperscalers cannot cover with their internal funds. In addition, 
the share of AI-related stocks in the portfolio of hedge funds conducting global equity investment 
has been increasing. If expectations regarding the profitability of AI -related investment were to 
decline, shocks could be amplified, mainly through portfolio adjustments in the foreign NBFI sector, 
and the effects could spill over to Japan.  With regard to major banks' overseas lending, although 
lending to foreign funds and data centers accounts  for a limited share of total overseas lending, 
these areas have become focus segments for major banks, reflecting factors such as high interest 
rate spreads. Banks engaged in such lending need to carefully manage the quality of their portfolios.

expectations regarding the profitability of AI -related investment and assumes the situation where 
shocks are amplified mainly by portfolio adjustments in the NBFI sector . Based on the results, it 
can be judged that the stability of Japan's financial system is maintained. However, it is necessary

Firms' and households' credit costs → Chapters IV-A, V-A, and Box 1 
Although above pre-pandemic levels, corporate bankruptcies and default rates have been more or 
less unchanged (left panel of Chart I-5). Examining the distribution of the ratio of operating profits 
to sales for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), there are substantial disparities across 
firms. The ratio of operating profits to sales has improved steadily among SMEs in the upper range 
of the distribution, while the ratio for those in the lower range has remained broadly unchanged in 
negative territory (middle panel of Chart I-5). Large-scale disruptions in supply chains have been 
avoided in the wake of the situation in the Middle East, partly due to progress in securing alternative 
sources of supply. Nevertheless, developments such as the rise in raw material and energy prices 
appear to be exerting downward pressure on profits, particularly at SMEs. An examination of the 
effects of a hypothetical 100 percent rise in crude oil prices on the probabilities of default of SMEs 
shows that the share of SMEs experiencing an increase in the ir probabilities of default is overall 
limited. However, it should be noted that, among SMEs with cost structures that tend to be  
susceptible to the effects of the rise in crude oil prices , some exhibit relatively large increases in 
their probabilities of default (right panel of Chart I-5).

Advances in so -called "frontier AI" have further heightened cybersecurity threats, as they could 
increase the speed and scale of cyberattacks.  Cyber incidents not only pose a risk to individual 
financial institutions and their customers but are also a material risk from a macroprudential

necessary to further enhance the resilience of individual financial institutions and the financial

continue to closely monitor the impact on the financial system of various risk-taking activities by

A. Global financial markets during the first half of fiscal 2026 
With regard to developments in global financial markets during the first half of fiscal 2026, the 
expansion in global AI -related demand had the effect of improving market sentiment, although 
uncertainties remained high over the situation in the Middle East. Against this background, stock 
prices increased, and credit spreads on corporate bonds remained at low levels. Nonetheless, 
stock prices saw adjustments at times, reflecting market attention to the high valuation of AI-related 
stocks. 
U.S. and European bond markets 
U.S. long -term interest rates  rose substantially, driven by factors such as  increased market 
expectations of policy interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve, amid higher inflationary pressure 
stemming from the situation in the Middle East  (Chart II-1-1). The yield curve for U.S. Treasuries 
also rose across a wide range of maturities. European long-term interest rates increased in tandem 
with U.S. interest rates, as attention was drawn to heightened inflationary pressure stemming from 
the situation in the Middle East. Implied volatilities of government bond futures for the United States 
and Germany declined as a trend, but thereafter rose again through the end of September.

A. Global financial markets during the first half of fiscal 2026

U.S. and European credit markets 
In U.S. and European credit markets, credit spreads on corporate bonds narrowed slightly due to 
the improvement in market sentiment, despite a substantial increase in issuance, mainly by AI-
related firms (left panel of Chart II-1-3). Looking at the distribution of credit spreads on U.S. high-
yield bonds, the overall level of spreads  remained low (middle panel of Chart II-1-3). Meanwhile, 
the default rate s on high-yield bonds remained more or less unchanged.  The default rates on 
leveraged loans were on a declining trend but remained at relatively high levels due to factors such 
as the cumulative effects of the high interest rate environment (right panel of Chart II-1-3). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Emerging markets and international commodity markets

C. Risks to financial markets 
Uncertainty in financial markets remains high. Specifically, attention is focus ed on uncertainties 
regarding the future course of the situation in the Middle East and its effects on economic activity 
and prices at home and abroad. Market participants have also been paying attention to 
developments in global AI-related demand and the course of fiscal and monetary policies in each 
jurisdiction. 
In stock markets, attention is needed to the risk that, depending on the future course of the situation 
in the Middle East,  heightened concerns over a global economic slowdown and over inflationary 
pressure could cause a deterioration in market sentiment . In addition,  amid uncertainty over 
whether AI -related profit growth will materialize, caution regarding the risk of stock price 
adjustments remains high. In bond markets, market participants have focused their attention on the 
future conduct of monetary policy and developments in fiscal policy in each jurisdiction, in addition 
to the effects of increased tension over the situation in the Middle East. In credit markets, attention 
continues to focus on  the easing of supply and demand conditions resulting from increased 
issuance of corporate bonds and other securities by AI -related firms , and on uncertainty over 
whether their profits will expand in line with strong business fixed investment , as well as  on the 
cumulative effects of the high  interest rate environment in the United States and Europe  on the 
financial conditions of firms with low credit ratings and those with high leverage ratios . In this 
situation, if concerns over private funds grow, there is a risk that credit spreads will widen through 
a decline in market participants' risk tolerance. 
In emerging markets, there have been concerns over the risk of capital outflows from countries with 
fiscal and financial vulnerabilities, as attention has continued to be paid to the possibility that the 
future course of the situation in the Middle East could exert downward pressure on economic activity. 
In particular, stock prices in economies where AI-related stocks account for a large share of the 
stock market  could fluctuate significantly due to developments in AI -related business fixed 
investment. In international commodity markets, attention is warranted regarding the risk that the 
surge in commodity prices -- such as those of crude oil -- could be prolonged reflecting the situation 
in the Middle East, as well as uncertainty over developments in the Chinese economy, which have 
a significant impact on commodity and grain prices. 
Attention should continue to be paid to the possibility that the materialization of these risks could 
lead to a tightening in global financial conditions through such factors as a sharp repricing of risky 
assets and a deterioration in the dollar funding environment.

The effects of the rise in raw material and energy prices on the financial positions and 
default probabilities of SMEs 
This section examines the effects of the rise in  raw material and energy prices re flecting the 
situation in the Middle East on  the financial positions and default probabilities of SMEs, mainly 
using firm-level financial data for SMEs. 
First, estimates based on input -output tables indicate that the rise in crude oil prices would be 
passed through to prices in a broad range of sectors, particularly the energy sector and 
intermediate goods such as chemical products (left panel of Chart IV-1-5). An examination of cost 
structures by industry, taking account of these spillover effects, shows that, in addition to electricity 
and gas as well as transportation -- where energy accounts for a large share of input costs -- 
manufacturing and construction are also susceptible to rises in crude oil prices (right panel of Chart 
IV-1-5).  
Next, using firm -level financial data for SMEs, the impact of higher intermediate -input costs 
triggered by a hypothetical 100 percent rise in crude oil prices on the financial positions of SMEs is 
examined. Holding all else equal, including the price pass -through rate, higher intermediate-input 
prices worsen firms' financial positions by squeezing operating profits.

i Objectives of the Financial System Report The Bank of Japan's Financial System Report has two main objectives. The first is to assess the stability of Japan's financial system. The second is to communicate with all related parties on the future tasks and challenges in order to ensure the system's stability. The Report assesses the vulnerabilities of the financial system from a macroprudential perspective. Within a macroprudential framework, institutional designs and policy measures are developed based on risk assessments in the financial system in order to ensure the stability of the overall financial system. In so doing, the interconnectedness of the real economy, financial markets, and financial institutions' behavior is taken into account. The Bank uses the results of the analysis set out in the Report in planning policies to ensure the stability of the financial system a nd for providing guidance and advice to financial institutions through on-site examinations and off-site monitoring. It makes use of the results in international discussions on regulation, supervision, and vulnerability assessment. In relation to the conduct of monetary policy, the macro assessment of financial system stability is also regarded as important input for the Bank in assessing risks in economic and price developments from a medium- to long- term perspective. Motivations behind the October 2026 issue In global and domestic financial markets, the expansion in global AI-related demand had the effect of improving market sentiment, although uncertainties remained high over the situation in the Middle East. Against this background, stock prices increased, and credit spreads on corporate bonds remained at low levels. However, uncertainties remain high over factors such as the future situation in the Middle East, the profitability and financing of AI -related investment, and developments in the foreign non-bank financial intermediary (NBFI) sector. This Report assesses the stability of the financial

system under such an external environment. With regard to the foreign NBFI sector , private funds and other entities have been playing an increasingly prominent role as providers of financing amid the substantial increase in global AI- related investment. This Report examines these recent developments and, in its macro stress testing, refines the specification of the impact of a decline in expectations regarding the profitability of AI-related investment and assumes the situation where shocks are amplified mainly by portfolio adjustments in the foreign NBFI sector, thereby assessing the adequacy of banks' capital. While no major financial imbalances have been seen in the domestic financial cycle, developments in asset prices, such as real estate prices and stock prices, continue to warrant careful attention and close monitoring. Furthermore, the Report examines the effects of the rise in raw material and energy prices reflecting the situation in the Middle East on small and medium -sized enterprises (SMEs), as well as the effects of interest rate increases on the corporate and household sectors . In addition, it assesses banks' profits and loss-absorbing capacity during the phase of policy rate hikes and examines issues surrounding loan and deposit management. Moreover, given that advances in so -called "frontier AI" have further heightened cybersecurity threats, this Report reviews the efforts undertaken by financial institutions, financial authorities, and other relevant entities.

I. Executive summary: Stability assessment of Japan's financial system 1 I. Executive summary: Stability assessment of Japan's financial system Japan's financial system has been maintaining stability on the whole. In the loan market, financial intermediation has continued to function smoothly as firms' demand for loans has continued to rise and banks' lending stance has remained active. Under these circumstances, no major financial imbalances have been seen in current financial activities. Japanese banks have sufficient capital bases and stable funding bases to withstand various stress situations, specifically including (1) stress equivalent to the global financial crisis that would cause major corrections in financial markets and the real economy at home and abroad ; and (2) a compound stress of the materialization of geopolitical risks such as a rise in crude oil prices, together with a decline in expectations regarding AI, and a substantial rise in interest rates, all happening simultaneously. However, it is necessary to continue to carefully monitor the impact that factors such as the future situation in the Middle East, the profitability and financing of AI-related investment, and developments in the foreign non-bank financial intermediary (NBFI) sector have on the financial system through various channels . From a long -term perspective, if a structural decline in firms' loan demand, mainly reflecting the population decline, persists, banks' profitability and loss-absorbing capacity could decline, depending on the supply and demand balance in the loan market. This could lead to a contraction of financial intermediation activities or an overheating, such as an excessive search for yield. From the perspective of maintaining stability in Japan's financial system , close attention is warranted on future developments in the system, while examining both overheating and contraction risks (Chart I-1). Executive summary: Stability assessment of Japan's financial system 3 Foreign NBFI sector and AI-related investment → Chapters III, IV-A, V-B, and VI-B The presence of the foreign NBFI sector has expanded globally, raising concerns about risks such as the amplification of shocks in the event of stress. Although the share of financial assets held by the domestic NBFI sector in Japan is relatively low compared with other countries, there has been a steady increase in lending to and investment in the foreign NBFI sector by domestic banks, as well as in investments in Japanese stocks and bonds by the foreign NBFI sector, particularly those related to foreign funds (left panel of Chart I-4). Against this background, Japan's financial system may have become more susceptible to fluctuations in global financial markets and developments in foreign investment funds. Driven by strong expectations for growth in AI -related markets, hyperscalers , particularly in the United States , have significantly increased their business fixed investment recently. While hyperscalers have traditionally financed data center investment with their internal funds, they have recently increased external financing mainly through corporate bond issuance and have increasingly sought to secure rights to use third -party data centers via long -term lease commitments (middle and right panels of Chart I -4). Against this background, foreign NBFIs, including private funds, have been playing an increasingly prominent role as providers of financing for the part of such investment that hyperscalers cannot cover with their internal funds. In addition, the share of AI-related stocks in the portfolio of hedge funds conducting global equity investment has been increasing. If expectations regarding the profitability of AI -related investment were to decline, shocks could be amplified, mainly through portfolio adjustments in the foreign NBFI sector, and the effects could spill over to Japan. With regard

to major banks' overseas lending, although lending to foreign funds and data centers accounts for a limited share of total overseas lending, these areas have become focus segments for major banks, reflecting factors such as high interest rate spreads. Specifically, attention is focus ed on uncertainties regarding the future course of the situation in the Middle East and its effects on economic activity and prices at home and abroad. Market participants have also been paying attention to developments in global AI-related demand and the course of fiscal and monetary policies in each jurisdiction. In stock markets, attention is needed to the risk that, depending on the future course of the situation in the Middle East, heightened concerns over a global economic slowdown and over inflationary pressure could cause a deterioration in market sentiment . In addition, amid uncertainty over whether AI -related profit growth will materialize, caution regarding the risk of stock price adjustments remains high. In bond markets, market participants have focused their attention on the future conduct of monetary policy and developments in fiscal policy in each jurisdiction, in addition to the effects of increased tension over the situation in the Middle East. In credit markets, attention continues to focus on the easing of supply and demand conditions resulting from increased issuance of corporate bonds and other securities by AI -related firms , and on uncertainty over whether their profits will expand in line with strong business fixed investment , as well as on the cumulative effects of the high interest rate environment in the United States and Europe on the financial conditions of firms with low credit ratings and those with high leverage ratios . In this situation, if concerns over private funds grow, there is a risk that credit spreads will widen through a decline in market participants' risk tolerance. In emerging markets, there have been concerns over the risk

of capital outflows from countries with fiscal and financial vulnerabilities, as attention has continued to be paid to the possibility that the future course of the situation in the Middle East could exert downward pressure on economic activity. In particular, stock prices in economies where AI-related stocks account for a large share of the stock market could fluctuate significantly due to developments in AI -related business fixed investment. In international commodity markets, attention is warranted regarding the risk that the surge in commodity prices -- such as those of crude oil -- could be prolonged reflecting the situation in the Middle East, as well as uncertainty over developments in the Chinese economy, which have a significant impact on commodity and grain prices. Attention should continue to be paid to the possibility that the materialization of these risks could lead to a tightening in global financial conditions through such factors as a sharp repricing of risky assets and a deterioration in the dollar funding environment.

Examining the distribution of the ratio of operating profits to sales for SMEs, there are substantial disparities across firms. Abstracting from short-term fluctuations, the ratio of operating profits to sales has improved steadily among SMEs in the upper range of the distribution, while the ratio for those in the lower range has remained broadly unchanged in negative territory (right panel of Chart IV -1-4). Against this background, large -scale disruptions in supply chains have been avoided in the wake of the situation in the Middle East, partly due to progress in securing alternative sources of supply. Nevertheless, developments such as the rise in raw material and energy prices appear to be exerting downward pressure on profits, particularly at SMEs. The effects of the rise in raw material and energy prices on the financial positions and default probabilities of SMEs This section examines the effects of the rise in raw material and energy prices re flecting the situation in the Middle East on the financial positions and default probabilities of SMEs, mainly using firm-level financial data for SMEs. First, estimates based on input -output tables indicate that the rise in crude oil prices would be passed through to prices in a broad range of sectors, particularly the energy sector and intermediate goods such as chemical products (left panel of Chart IV-1-5). An examination of cost structures by industry, taking account of these spillover effects, shows that, in addition to electricity and gas as well as transportation -- where energy accounts for a large share of input costs -- manufacturing and construction are also susceptible to rises in crude oil prices (right panel

of Chart IV-1-5). Next, using firm -level financial data for SMEs, the impact of higher intermediate -input costs triggered by a hypothetical 100 percent rise in crude oil prices on the financial positions of SMEs is examined. Holding all else equal, including the price pass -through rate, higher intermediate-input prices worsen firms' financial positions by squeezing operating profits. IV. Risks faced by financial institutions A. Credit risk 33 of lending t o SMEs also show that financially vulnerable firms tend to have longer remaining maturities. The longer remaining maturities of financially vulnerable firms may reflect the effects of COVID-19-related loans, including loans covered by refinancing guarantees (Chart IV -1-11). Although principal and interest payments on COVID -19-related loans are expected to proceed gradually, these loans are likely, for the time being, to partially mitigate the effects of recent interest rate increases on the corporate sector. Credit risks of common exposures Although banks' credit costs have remained limited, recent developments show that there have been some cases where banks have recorded large credit costs on "common exposures," i.e., loans to the same borrowers by multiple banks. When banks have common exposures, their loan portfolios are more likely to be synchronized in the event of a shock. Such common exposures have expanded, reflecting an increase in lending by primarily regional banks to "non-main-bank borrowing firms," that is, to firms for which the lending bank is not the main bank and an increase in "cross-prefecture" lending -- that is, loans to prefectures other than their head office locations.13 In general, banks that are not a firm's main bank may find it more difficult than the firm's main bank to obtain timely and appropriate information on the firm. Such information gaps can lead to differences in the borrower classifications assigned by banks to the same firm.
